strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: A chauffeur company takes New York to court over the trip log, and the movements of the wealthy become a constitutional question
lead.standfirst: Wheely argues that a city rule requiring every journey to be recorded to within three feet, and then kept indefinitely, quietly builds a permanent surveillance file on the people it drives.
lead.body:
The rule at the centre of the case is administrative rather than dramatic. Every licensed for-hire vehicle operator in New York City must submit a monthly, unaggregated record of each trip taken. That record includes pickup and drop-off locations to within three feet, the exact timing of the journey, and driver and vehicle details. The data is retained indefinitely. Wheely, a chauffeur service founded in London in 2012 and now operating in Paris, Dubai and New York, went to court almost as soon as it entered the New York market in the spring, arguing that the requirement amounts to a warrantless and permanent record of its clients' movements. A judge in the Southern District of New York dismissed the claim in April 2026. The case is now before the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.

Anton Chirkunov, the company's chief executive, told Spear's that the exposure is not evenly distributed. "Privacy is an asymmetrical risk for the wealthy," he said, citing doxxing and the consequences of government data being shared, leaked or stolen. "A record of a person's rides is a record of their life," he added, pointing to the business meetings they take, the homes they return to and the schools their children attend. The New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission says the trip log rule is necessary to enforce driver fatigue and passenger safety requirements, and that it takes its responsibility to protect the data seriously.

The precedent that hangs over the argument is a decade old. In 2014 the city released 173 million taxi trip records under a public records request. The records were not sufficiently anonymised, and researchers were able to reverse the process using publicly available photographs and celebrity gossip blogs. One analyst traced a specific 2013 ride taken by the actor Bradley Cooper, down to a fare of USD 10.50 with no recorded tip. The episode is remembered as a curiosity. The lesson underneath it is that a large enough movement dataset does not stay anonymous for long.

Security practitioners describe a more serious version of the same problem. Mike O'Neill, managing director of the security firm Optimal Risk, told Spear's that repeated pickup and drop-off locations can be analysed to identify a client's home address, office, family residences, schools and gyms with a high degree of confidence. Once that pattern is established, he said, a threat actor can begin to predict where an individual is likely to be at a specific date and time. He warned that agentic artificial intelligence tools could automate this kind of pattern analysis at scale, creating openings for surveillance, stalking and kidnapping, and making burglary less risky during known absences. Cameron Colquhoun, chief executive of the cybersecurity firm Neon Century, added that with the right open source intelligence, anonymised data can be reverse engineered relatively easily.

Wheely's own model reads as a catalogue of private service discipline. Drivers train at what the company calls a chauffeur academy, sign non-disclosure agreements, and operate without CCTV inside the vehicle. Chirkunov says clients speak on the telephone in the car in a way they do not in conventional black cars. The company withdrew its product from app stores in Russia in 2020 rather than comply with local data rules, and Chirkunov says he is prepared to take the New York challenge to the Supreme Court. "The question is not whether it leaks," he said, "but when."
lead.why: A family's movements are now a dataset, and someone in the household creates it every day by booking cars, flights and school runs. Knowing which suppliers record, retain and sell journey data is becoming as much a part of the role as knowing which florist to call.

articles.title: Three in four family businesses have been attacked, and the people who answer the telephone are now part of the defence
articles.body:
Deloitte Private's Family business cybersecurity 2026, published on 29 January as part of its family business insights series, puts a number on something the private world has preferred to discuss quietly. Nearly three quarters of family businesses globally, 74 per cent, have faced at least one cyberattack in the past two years. A third, 33 per cent, have experienced two or more. Exposure is close to universal by region. Asia Pacific leads on frequency with 90 per cent reporting at least one attack, North America follows at 77 per cent, and even the lowest region, South America, records 61 per cent.

The shape of those attacks matters more to a household than the headline. Malware was reported by 49 per cent of respondents and phishing or business email compromise by 48 per cent, but the next three categories are the ones that arrive through people rather than through servers. Social engineering was experienced by 43 per cent, third-party risk by 40 per cent and insider threats by 27 per cent. Each of those routes runs through someone who has been trusted with access: a supplier, a contractor, an assistant, a member of staff.

Defences have not kept pace. Only 43 per cent of family businesses report a robust cybersecurity strategy that has never failed them. Of the rest, 49 per cent describe a strategy with noticeable gaps and 8 per cent have none at all, and 48 per cent feel only moderately prepared or not at all prepared should an attack land. Basic controls are widespread: software updates at 59 per cent, network security and multi-factor authentication at 57 per cent each, data backups at 48 per cent. The more advanced measures lag badly. Incident response playbooks appear in 40 per cent of cases, cyber maturity assessments in 36 per cent, vendor governance in 32 per cent and identity management in 31 per cent.

The consequences are now routine rather than exceptional. Among those targeted, 54 per cent suffered financial harm, 51 per cent operational harm and 51 per cent reputational harm. Only 4 per cent of respondents globally reported no loss or damage of any kind. For a family that owns the business, the reputational column is not an abstraction, because the family name is the brand and the household is where the family name lives.

The practical translation for private service is narrow and useful. Vendor governance and identity management are the two weakest controls in the survey, and both are exercised daily inside a house: who is on the approved supplier list, who is admitted, who is given a code, who is allowed to change a bank detail on an invoice. A household that verifies payment instructions by voice on a known number, keeps a written contractor register and rehearses what happens when a convincing message arrives at nine on a Friday evening is running a control the family business itself may not have.
articles.why: Social engineering and third-party risk reach the household long before they reach the family office. The person who checks a payment instruction, verifies a delivery or refuses an unscheduled contractor is operating a security control, not performing a courtesy.

articles.title: Hackers copy Liechtenstein's register of beneficial owners, and the names behind 31,000 structures walk out of the door
articles.body:
During the night of 29 to 30 July, unknown perpetrators gained unauthorised access to Liechtenstein's register of beneficial owners and copied data relating to around 31,000 companies, foundations and trusts. Irregularities were detected and the affected system was taken offline. The government convened a crisis unit on the Saturday evening, headed by the prime minister, Brigitte Haas, and the minister of justice, Emanuel Schadler. On the current state of knowledge, there is no indication that data in the system was modified or deleted. It was copied.

The register itself was created in 2021, under Liechtenstein's Act on the Register of the Beneficial Owners of Legal Entities, and is maintained by the Office of Justice for the purpose of preventing money laundering and terrorist financing. Its whole design is to strip away layers of corporate opacity and record, in one place, the natural persons who ultimately stand behind a legal structure. That is exactly what makes the file valuable to anyone who should not have it.

Liechtenstein matters here out of all proportion to its size. The Principality is one of Europe's principal jurisdictions for private foundations and trust structures, instruments used by families to hold operating businesses, art, property and succession arrangements across generations. A register of beneficial owners in Vaduz is, in effect, an index of a certain kind of European and international private wealth, with names attached.

The breach lands in a season in which the private world has been arguing about who holds its data and how long they hold it. The trip log dispute in New York turns on the same principle, that information collected for a legitimate administrative purpose becomes a hazard the moment it is aggregated, retained and connected to an identity. Registers of this kind are mandated by law and cannot be opted out of, which removes the usual defence of choosing discreet suppliers.

For those who work close to a family, the immediate lesson is not technical. It is that the paper trail is now the exposed surface. A structure that is invisible in public can still be legible in a government file, and that file can be copied in a single night.
articles.why: Discretion has moved beyond what staff say to who holds the family's name in writing. Anyone who completes forms, engages suppliers or files documents on a family's behalf is deciding, in small increments, how many registers carry that name.

articles.title: Monaco's average price passes 57,000 euros a square metre, and the long-term renters finally decide to buy
articles.body:
Savills' Spotlight on Monaco 2026 records an average price of EUR 57,569 per square metre across the Principality, roughly GBP 4,600 per square foot. Larvotto has passed EUR 70,000 per square metre for the first time, around GBP 5,600 per square foot, a figure driven largely by units at Mareterra, the ultra-prime development launched in December 2024, entering the market. Kelcie Sellers, who leads global residential research at Savills, described the effect plainly: "This has rewritten the rule book on what is considered ultra-prime in Monaco."

The defining constraint has not changed. Monaco occupies just over two square kilometres, and Sellers says the pipeline for new construction is now "basically zero". Total transaction value held steady at EUR 5.9 billion, but that stability conceals a shift in where the activity sits. New build has receded and resale has taken over, rising sharply in both volume and value in 2025. Sellers characterises this as a return to normal after the Mareterra cycle, which she calls a temporary disruption in an otherwise resale-led market.

Within the resale segment, demand has concentrated on size. Four-bedroom homes have seen some of the strongest price appreciation, with average values rising more than 50 per cent, while ultra-prime resales above EUR 20 million reached record levels. Irene Luke, co-head of Savills Monaco, put the buyer logic simply: "The bigger the apartment, the better it is for buyers." She attributes the shift to Monaco's evolution from a fiscal base into a place people actually live. "Monaco has become a lot more sophisticated. The schooling is better, healthcare is better."

The supporting detail is domestic rather than financial. A new British school opened in 2022, alongside the established presence of the International School of Monaco. Nice airport, around 30 minutes away by road, keeps adding transatlantic routes and European links. Sellers notes that remote working convinced buyers they could run global businesses from the Principality, and they have been upgrading into larger homes accordingly.

The rental market is pushing in the same direction. Supply shortages have driven rents up more than 9 per cent over the past year, and properties are frequently secured before they reach the open market. Luke reports the consequence in client behaviour: "Long-term renters finally are thinking that they should really buy something."
articles.why: A four-bedroom principal residence occupied full time is a different brief from a pied-a-terre visited for the Grand Prix. It requires a rota, a supplier book, school-run logistics and a handover file, which is why Monaco households increasingly recruit for permanence rather than for the season.
articles.src: Savills, Spotlight on Monaco 2026, reported by Spear's

articles.title: 43 yachts delivered this year gather in Port Hercule, and the yards behind them are sold out to 2029
articles.body:
The Monaco Yacht Show has published the first official list of superyachts confirmed for its 35th edition, which runs in Port Hercule from 23 to 26 September. Around 120 vessels are expected by opening day, and 43 of the yachts on the initial list are due for delivery during 2026. Toby Moore, chief executive of Informa Prestige, which organises the show, framed the appeal in logistical terms: "In four days and in a single harbour, you can walk the decks of 43 yachts delivering this year."

The largest new delivery on the current list is the 102 metre Nixie, built by Lurssen, and the smallest is Arcadia's A80 at 23.98 metres. Between them sit Damen Yachting's 80 metre Pangea and 60 metre QU2, Sanlorenzo's 73.4 metre Silver Fox and Isa Yachts' 66.4 metre Sea Raider X. The segment from 40 to 60 metres is well represented, with Benetti's B.Now 50M, Riva's 54 Metri, Baglietto's Fast50 and T60, Tankoa's Singolare, Gulf Craft's Majesty 145 and Sirena Marine's Sirena Superyacht 42 Metre. Italian builders account for much of the confirmed fleet, including Sanlorenzo, Azimut-Benetti and brands within the Ferretti Group. Sailing yachts, multihulls, recently refitted vessels and brokerage yachts complete the list, with more names due before September.

The context behind the fleet is a market that is contracting in count and expanding in scale. BOAT International's Global Order Book 2026 reports that the number of yachts on order has declined for a second consecutive year, while average yacht size continues to increase and build slots at the leading shipyards are largely committed until 2028 to 2029. The industry is not building more boats. It is building bigger ones, and it has already sold the next three years of capacity.

That combination has a direct effect below deck. Every one of the 43 new hulls arriving this year requires a crew, an interior standard, a provisioning chain and a shoreside team, and larger average tonnage means larger complements per vessel. A fleet growing by size rather than by number still increases total demand for people, and it does so in the specific direction of senior, experienced crew capable of running a 60 metre programme rather than a 30 metre one.
articles.why: Yachts and houses draw on the same shrinking pool of trained private staff, and a rising average length means each new delivery absorbs more of it. For anyone building a career on the interior side, the growth is at the top of the size range, where standards and expectations are highest.

articles.title: Swiss watch exports hold at CHF 12.2 billion for the half year, and all the growth arrives at the bottom of the price list
articles.body:
The Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry published its half year statistics on 21 July. Exports of wristwatches declined slightly, by 0.6 per cent, to CHF 12.2 billion over the first six months of 2026. Volumes moved the other way. More than 7 million watches were shipped abroad in the period, an increase of 162,000 units on the first half of 2025, or 2.3 per cent. More watches left Switzerland, and they were worth marginally less.

The explanation sits in the price bands. Volume growth was driven mainly by mechanical watches with an export price below CHF 500, a category up 23.8 per cent. The drag on value came from the segment running from CHF 500 to CHF 3,000, down 5.7 per cent. The industry is selling more of its cheapest mechanical product and less of the middle, which is where a great deal of the industry's revenue traditionally lives.

The monthly pattern within the half is worth holding separately from the total. June was strong, with exports up 11.2 per cent to nearly CHF 2.4 billion and volumes up 11.7 per cent to 1.3 million pieces. That single month partly rescued a soft first quarter. The comparison base is a full year 2025 in which Swiss watch exports fell 1.7 per cent to CHF 25.5 billion, so a flat half year represents stabilisation rather than recovery.

This is a different signal from the one the salerooms have been sending. Auction results have been carried by trophy lots and by demand for independent makers, a narrow market of scarce pieces. The export figures describe the wide market of new product moving through retail, and the two can diverge for long periods. A collection can be appreciating while the industry that produced it is flat.

For anyone whose work touches a principal's collection, the useful discipline is to read both. Insurance valuations, service intervals and the question of whether a piece should be worn, stored or sold all sit at the intersection of a retail market that is soft in the middle and a secondary market that is selective at the top.
articles.why: Cultural fluency means being able to distinguish an auction headline from a trade statistic. A principal who mentions the watch market may be talking about either, and knowing which one is moving is part of holding the conversation properly.
articles.src: Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, half year statistics, 21 July 2026

briefs.b: A proposed maximum police response time of 20 minutes for rural emergencies could leave country estates exposed, security advisers have told Spear's, with organised crime groups increasingly targeting isolated houses, farms and outbuildings. The National Farmers' Union puts the cost of rural crime at GBP 44.1 million in 2025, down 16.5 per cent from GBP 52.8 million in 2023, a decline that greater police focus has driven but that the growing sophistication of those groups now threatens.

Aldar has activated the final phase of the Saadiyat Island masterplan with Marsa Al Saadiyat, a waterfront district carrying a gross development value of AED 100 billion, around USD 27.2 billion. It covers 6.4 million square metres, is planned for more than 58,000 residents across private mansions, villas, waterfront apartments and branded residences, and includes a marina with more than 350 berths. The first homes go on sale in the second half of 2026.

Yachts above 50 metres were largely committed for July and August by early spring, and berths in Monaco, Saint-Tropez, Porto Cervo and Mykonos are secured well in advance of the season. Brokers report demand outpacing supply in Mallorca, Ibiza, the Amalfi Coast and the Cyclades, with June and September offering similar conditions and considerably more flexibility on where a boat can stop.

Bvlgari Resort Ranfushi is due to open in Raa Atoll in the Maldives, around 45 minutes by seaplane from Male, across roughly 20 hectares. The property is planned with 54 villas and suites in total, including 33 beach villas with private pools, 20 overwater villas and a Bulgari Villa set on its own island. It is the group's tenth hotel and only its second resort.
